# Kuṇālajātaka (Ja 536)

**ID:** Ja 536  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Kuṇālajātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul4.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul4.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kuṇālajātaka* (Ja 536) is framed around a story told by the Buddha while staying beside Lake Kuṇāla to five hundred monks who were afflicted with discontent. It occupies an exceptional position within the Pali Jātaka collection because it is the only Jātaka to preserve canonical prose alongside verse, as attested by the presence of a dedicated word commentary explaining both its prose and verse portions [Kingsbury 2002; Norman 1983; Appleton 2010]. This canonical prose consists of narrative sections and elaborate descriptive passages marked by unusually long compound words depicting the sylvan beauty of the Himavat mountains [Collins 1998; Norman 1983], much of it composed in an archaic rhythmical style identified as *vedha* [Norman 2006]. The canonical prose begins with the pratīka *evam akkhāyati* [Norman 1983].

Substantively, the text comprises an atypical cycle of sub-stories and verses that dwell on the wickedness, treachery, and fickleness of women [Norman 1983; Harvey 2000; Shyu 2008]. Scholars observe that many of these verses represent pan-Indian secular misogynous gnomic literature rather than specifically Buddhist teachings [Norman 1983; Harvey 2000]. In contrast to the Pali version's pervasive ascetic misogyny, the parallel narrative preserved as story 62 in the Chinese *Liu du ji jing*, as well as a later thirteenth-century Sinhalese derivative, lacks misogynous tendencies entirely [Harvey 2000; Shyu 2008]. Text-critical analysis suggests that individual stanzas, such as the unique śloka *sabbā nadī…* among a run of triṣṭubh verses, represent early interpolations [von Hinüber 1994], while thematic parallels have been noted with the Sanskrit *Avimāraka* drama [Nakamura 1980]. A major critical edition and study utilizing manuscript evidence from the commentary and sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) was published by W. B. Bollée in 1970 [Norman 1983; Appleton 2010; von Hinüber 1994].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Passage-level parallels: Ja 341 Kaṇḍarījātaka; Ja 464 Cūḷakuṇālajātaka; Ja 61 Asātamantajātaka
- Mentioned in: Mil 5.4.8 Amarādevīpañha

**Sources**

- [Kingsbury 2002] Paul Kingsbury, The Chronology of the Pali Canon (2002) — Noted that Ja 536 uniquely contains canonical prose with its own commentary.
- [Collins 1998] Steven Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities (1998) — Discussed the poetic descriptions of Himavat and sylvan beauty using long compounds in the canonical prose.
- [Shyu 2008] Ching-mei Shyu, A Few Good Women: A Study of the Liu Du Ji Jing (2008) — Analyzed the misogynous themes of Ja 536 in comparison with the women-friendly parallel in Liu du ji jing no. 62.
- [Norman 1983] K. R. Norman, Pāli Literature (1983) — Detailed the unique canonical narrative and descriptive prose, the pratīka 'evam akkhāyati', non-Buddhist gnomic verses on women, and Bollée's edition using the ṭīkā.
- [Harvey 2000] Peter Harvey, An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics (2000) — Discussed the atypical form of the text, non-Buddhist misogynist verse parallels, and absence of misogyny in parallel versions.
- [Nakamura 1980] Hajime Nakamura, Indian Buddhism: A Survey with Bibliographical Notes (1980) — Noted literary parallels between the Kuṇālajātaka and the Avimāraka drama.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravāda Buddhism (2010) — Noted the presence of canonical prose in Ja 536 and Bollée's 1970 edition and translation.
- [Norman 2006] K. R. Norman, A Philological Approach to Buddhism (1997/2006) — Identified the archaic rhythmical vedha prose style in the canonical prose passages.
- [von Hinüber 1994] Oskar von Hinüber, Selected Papers on Pali Studies (1994) — Discussed the interpolation of the śloka verse sabbā nadī and cited Bollée's 1970 edition on botanical descriptions.
